headline: Race at 2.1 knots on the neap: bass off Valiant, slack at 13:50
subhead: Current's soft this week but Valiant Rock still gave up wire-line bass on the drop, and the first albie scouts are due any day now.
body_markdown:
Two-point-one knots. That's what I had running through the Race on Tuesday's max ebb, which tells you everything about why the bite's been a grind instead of a slam-dunk. We're deep in the neap cycle right now, moon's past the quarter, and the current through the Race, Plum Gut, and the Sluiceway has gone soft compared to what we run during the new and full moon springs. When the Race isn't ripping four-plus knots, the bait doesn't get pinned against the rock faces the same way, and the bass don't have to commit the way they do when the water's screaming.\n\nStill fished it. Still caught them. Slack at Valiant Rock ran 13:50 Tuesday, and I had the boat set up forty-five minutes ahead of that on the last of the ebb, wire line out with bunker spoons and a 36-ounce parachute jig working the down-current side where the rock breaks the flow. Marked bass sitting 38 to 44 feet down, right on the color line where the cold Race water meets the warmer push coming off Fishers Island Sound. Landed three keepers in the 28-32 inch range and lost a better fish — probably mid-30s — that came off right at the boat after a long fight in that heavy water. Nothing that'll make the wall, but solid, honest fish, and exactly the class you'd expect on a neap tide when the biggest fish are holding deeper and feeding more on the slow build than the max flow.\n\nPlum Gut has been the more interesting story. Water's holding around 69 to 70 degrees on the western approach and there's noticeably more bait stacked in the Gut than there was two weeks ago — pods of sand eels and some early snapper blues mixed in, which is exactly the forage albies want when they show. I haven't had a confirmed false albacore in the Gut yet, but I said last week to watch for early sign filtering into this zone as warm water pushed east along the Sound's outer edge, and that's precisely what's setting up. The thermal gradient from Kings Point in the low 70s down through New London in the high 60s means the warm water is stacking against the eastern Sound structure, and Plum Gut sits right at that seam. If you're itching to be first on albies this season, I'd be working epoxy jigs and small Deadly Dicks off the Gut's western edge on the last two hours of the ebb, when the current compresses the bait against structure and pushes it out toward Orient Point. Nothing landed yet — but the pattern is exactly what precedes the first scout schools in this zone historically, and Montauk and Block Island are reporting the same warming trend from the east.

Little Gull and Great Gull Island have been quieter than I'd like this week. I worked the rip off Great Gull twice with bucktails — white and chartreuse, 2 to 3 ounces depending on the drift speed — and only picked up bluefish, but they were good ones, 4 to 6 pounds, slashing hard on the surface during the last hour of daylight both nights. That fits the coastwide pattern right now — bluefish are the most reliable visible story on the whole East Coast, working bunker schools relentlessly from Jersey up through the Sound, and our fish are part of that same push. If you want non-stop bent rods with less technical current work, that's your play: find the bunker schools showing on the surface off Great Gull or along the Sluiceway edge, and throw metal — Kastmasters or Hopkins — right into the boil.

The Sluiceway itself fished tough. That channel needs current to be worth the trip, and on a 2-knot day it just doesn't set up the same edges and eddies that concentrate bait. I made one pass through there Wednesday morning and didn't mark enough bait to justify staying, so I pulled out and ran back to Valiant. Lesson for anybody planning a trip this week — check the current tables before you commit to the Sluiceway specifically. It's a springs-tide spot. On the neap, your time is better spent at Valiant Rock or the Race itself where the rock structure still concentrates fish even with reduced flow.

Fluke have been a non-factor for me this week, which tracks with what's happening across the Sound generally — warm shallow water has pushed the better fish deeper, and I haven't had the bottom time to specifically target them with everything else going on. If you want fluke, I'd look at the deeper edges around Race Rock itself on a stronger tide stage, working Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails tight to bottom, but it's not been my focus.

Sea bass on the reef structure around Valiant and out toward the Sluiceway approach have been steady and reliable — not exciting, but a good option if the rip isn't cooperating. Squid strips or clam on bottom rigs in 40-50 feet has produced consistent keepers.

Looking ahead: the current rebuilds through the weekend as we move away from the neap and toward the next quarter, and that's when I expect the Race and Plum Gut to wake back up to their full potential. Slack at Valiant next week should run a few minutes later each day — I'll have exact windows once I check the tables again — but the bigger story is the albies. Water's warming on schedule, bait's staging in the Gut, and every signal from Montauk and Block Island east of us says the first confirmed albacore should hit this corridor within the week. I'd keep a rod rigged with small epoxy jigs ready to go on short notice. When they show in the Gut, it happens fast and it happens all at once.
